sections.b: After the Sermon on the Mount Matthew sets ten miracles in three groups, with sayings between: a man with skin disease, a centurion's servant and Peter's mother-in-law (8:1–17); the storm, two men with demons and a paralyzed man (8:23–9:8); an official's daughter, a bleeding woman, two blind men and a man who could not speak (9:18–34). They show Jesus' authority by word and touch, and end with the crowd's wonder and the Pharisees' charge that he works by the ruler of demons (9:33–34). In chapter 10 Jesus gives the Twelve the same authority (10:1, 8).

common: Matthew shortens Mark's miracle stories to put the focus on Jesus' words and the people's faith.

sections.b: Matthew sees Jesus' healings as fulfilling Isaiah 53:4, translated from the Hebrew to speak of bodily sickness. Pentecostal and Holiness teaching drew from this the doctrine of healing in the atonement; others read the verse as fulfilled in Jesus' ministry, with full healing promised at the resurrection. In the bleeding woman's story Matthew uses "save" for healing three times (9:21–22), tying bodily rescue to salvation.

uncommon: A few scholars think Matthew deliberately avoided the Septuagint's spiritualizing of Isaiah 53:4 to keep its plain bodily meaning.

sections.h: Jesus and the man with skin disease
sections.b: In Matthew 8:1–4 a man with lepra, the Greek for tsara'at, asks to be made clean. Jesus touches him and then sends him to the priest with the offering of Leviticus 14, keeping the Law. The Twelve are sent to cleanse such people too (10:8).

sections.h: The Son of Man in Matthew 8–10
sections.b: The title first appears in Matthew at 8:20, of a homeless Jesus, then at 9:6, with authority to forgive sins on earth, and at 10:23, of his future coming. These three uses already show the range of the title in Matthew: humble life, present authority, coming glory (Daniel 7:13–14).

sections.h: "Only to the lost sheep of Israel" and "all nations"
sections.b: Matthew alone records Jesus' command to the Twelve not to go to Gentiles or Samaritans (10:5–6), and alone ends with the command to make disciples of all nations (28:19). Readers explain the tension as two stages (Israel first, as in Romans 1:16), as history in Matthew's community, or as Jesus' expectation that the nations would come at the end. The saying that "the sons of the kingdom will be thrown out" (8:12) was long used to claim that the church replaced Israel; within Matthew the same warning is aimed at his own church (13:38–42; 22:11–14).
sections.refs: Matthew 10:5–6; Matthew 15:24; Matthew 28:19; Matthew 8:11–12; Matthew 13:38–42; Romans 1:16

sections.h: "Mercy is what I want" (Hosea 6:6 in Matthew)
sections.b: Only Matthew has Jesus quote Hosea 6:6, twice: to defend eating with sinners (9:13) and his disciples' Sabbath plucking (12:7). Hosea's word is hesed, loyal love. Rabbinic tradition also made the verse central after the Temple's fall, when Yohanan ben Zakkai taught that acts of loving-kindness atone as sacrifice did.

When John's disciples ask why Jesus' followers do not fast, Jesus answers that guests do not fast at a wedding, but will fast when the groom is taken away (Matthew 9:14–15). The Torah required one fast a year; Pharisees and John's disciples kept extra fasts, and early Christians fasted on Wednesdays and Fridays (Didache 8:1).

The woman who had bled for twelve years touched the kraspedon of Jesus' cloak (Matthew 9:20), the tassel commanded in Numbers 15:38–40. Jesus wore the tassels of an observant Jew; others sought to touch them too (Matthew 14:36), and he criticized those who lengthened them for show (Matthew 23:5).

Jesus sees the crowds "like sheep that have no shepherd" (Matthew 9:36), Moses' words in Numbers 27:17, and sends the Twelve to "the sheep of the house of Israel that are lost" (10:6), echoing Jeremiah 50:6 and Ezekiel 34. He sends them out "like sheep" among wolves (10:16).
sections.refs: Matthew 9:36; Matthew 10:6; Matthew 10:16; Numbers 27:17; Ezekiel 34:5–16; Jeremiah 50:6

sections.b: In the prophets the harvest pictures judgment (Joel 3:13). In Matthew 9:37–38 Jesus turns the image to mission: the harvest is large, the workers few, and the disciples must ask the Lord of the harvest to send more, after which he sends them.

Matthew names the Twelve when Jesus sends them out, the only time he calls them "apostles" (10:2). He alone calls Peter "first" and Matthew "the tax collector," and he renders Simon's title as "the Cananaean," from the Aramaic for "zealous."

Jesus' choice of twelve, sent first to "the house of Israel" (Matthew 10:5–6), points to the hope that all twelve tribes would be gathered again; he promises the Twelve thrones judging the tribes (Matthew 19:28).

Jesus says a town that refuses his messengers will fare worse on judgment day than Sodom and Gomorrah (Matthew 10:15; compare 11:23–24). Jewish tradition remembered Sodom's cruelty to strangers (Wisdom of Solomon 19:13–15), which sharpens the comparison with towns that refuse hospitality to God's messengers.
sections.refs: Matthew 10:14–15; Matthew 11:23–24; Genesis 19:1–25; Ezekiel 16:49–50; Wisdom of Solomon 19:13–15

sections.b: The mission discourse prepares Jesus' messengers for courts, floggings and death (Matthew 10:17–22, 28) and promises that whoever confesses Jesus before people will be confessed before the Father (10:32–33). Early martyr accounts turn on this choice.

Jesus tells the Twelve they will not finish the towns of Israel before the Son of Man comes. Readings include a disappointed expectation (Schweitzer), the resurrection, the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70, and a continuing mission to Israel until the second coming.

sections.h: Destroying soul and body in Gehenna
sections.b: Jesus tells his messengers to fear the One who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna (Matthew 10:28). The verse is central in the debate between everlasting punishment and conditional immortality, and in Matthew's recurring image of weeping and grinding of teeth in the outer darkness (8:12).

The Pharisees say Jesus drives out demons by "the ruler of the demons" (Matthew 9:34); Jesus tells his disciples they have called the head of the house Beelzebul (10:25), a name that plays on zebul, "exalted house." The charge returns in full in 12:24–32.

Only this Gospel names the tax collector at Capernaum Matthew (9:9) and lists "Matthew the tax collector" among the Twelve (10:3); Mark and Luke call him Levi. Tradition sees the author's own story; many critical scholars see a change made to link the call to one of the Twelve.
